newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: East Asia Grain - South Korea still looking for feed wheat.
newsitem.headline: East Asia Grain - South Korea still looking for feed wheat.

text.p: South Korean buyers are expected to be in the market soon for 100,000 tonnes of feed wheat, but are also being tempted by falling prices of alternative corn, while Japanese buyers are staying away, local traders said on Monday.
Feed processors in South Korea still need to buy Canadian feed wheat to cover their requirements for February and March shipments, they said.
"South Korean buyers have to buy more than two 50,000-tonne cargoes of feed wheat a month for each of the February and March shipments," said a trader with Taihan Sugar Corp.
Last week, the biggest South Korean feed buyer, the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF), said it passed on a tender for 52,500 tonnes of feed wheat due to higher than expected prices.
An NLCF trader said the target price for the feed wheat was below $130 a tonne, C&F based on Canadian origin wheat.
He said the lowest bid for the passed tender was $139.25 a tonne C&F, if sourced from Canada. And the lowest bid for Australian-sourced wheat was $130.80 a tonne C&F.
The trader said the NLCF was considering changing its original plan to buy feed wheat and could substitute the wheat with corn if corn prices fall further.

A trader with a Seoul-based U.S. trading house said the freight premium to South Korean ports from the Pacific Northwest remained unchanged at between $13 to $14 a tonne, and the freight premium from the U.S. Gulf at $24 a tonne.

In Japan, grain importers said they were likely to remain sidelined this week as they await further price falls on the Chicago market following last week's bearish crop production report by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).
"We're looking for the right timing to buy U.S. corn for April-June shipment. But it looks better to wait for a further drop in corn prices," a major trade house official said.
"Given the bearish USDA report, we expect corn prices to fall further in the immediate term," he said.
The USDA forecast last week that the 1996 U.S. corn crop would total 9.265 million bushels, far above previous estimates.
Japanese importers have already bought more than 90 percent of their U.S. corn requirements for January/March shipment.
Premiums for U.S. corn are currently quoted at around 97 to 98 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade's March 1997 contract, traders said.
China -- lifting an export ban in effect since December 1994 -- is offering corn to some Japanese trade houses, but their prices are still too high, traders said.
"They are offering at about $150 (a tonne on an FOB basis). Considering the quality problem during deliveries, this price level is too high," one corn trader said.

Traders said they would soon start corn import negotiations for 1997 with Argentina, adding that imports from the South American country are likely to increase next year in an attempt to reduce Japan's dependence on the U.S. crop.
In the oilseeds market Japanese importers said they are gradually buying U.S. soybean for early February shipment.
